meta.title: Polish B1
meta.subtitle: 1,000 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Polish → English (see the Polish, recall the meaning) and English → Polish (see an English meaning, recall the Polish). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1,000 words for level B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Poland's State Commission for the Certification of Proficiency in Polish as a Foreign Language examines at all six levels, but no official word list was found for any of them. So 735 of the 1,000 words were written for Folio, a topic at a time, for the topics the B1 exam is described as covering — tastes and character, the family and its occasions, social life, sport, town and country and public institutions, travel, work and the labour market, education, recipes and cooking, shopping and ways of paying, health and way of life, the environment, the state and society (politics, the economy, crime), science and technology, the media, culture and stereotypes — together with the words for expressing surprise, doubt, sympathy, disappointment, criticism and advice, and the connectives of an argument. They are Folio's choice, not the Commission's, and this is not an official word list. No word taught in the levels below is repeated. The other 265 are the commonest words of everyday Polish not already chosen, from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles, each word counted over all its forms. The cards are ordered by that frequency, so the words met most often come first; the 21 set phrases, which a list of single words cannot count, come last. Polish changes the endings of its nouns, adjectives and verbs, and many stems change with them, so each card carries the forms that cannot be guessed, read from a dictionary rather than generated. 584 nouns show their gender, three cases of the singular and two of the plural. 250 verbs show their aspect and its partner, the forms for ja (I), on (he) and oni (they) and the past of on — a perfective verb's being its future, since it has no present. 32 adjectives show their comparative and superlative. One pronoun shows its cases. Real example sentences come with 907 of the 1,000 words, three apiece for 763, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Meanings, forms and parts of speech: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency ordering: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
